paras: The lynching of Charles Jackson was the killing of Charles W. Jackson, a Black man, by a mob of white men at 13th and Robey streets in Chicago on a Monday night, apparently June 30, 1919. His brother James Jackson was beaten by the mob and then arrested by police, and five members of the mob were reported shot. The Chicago Defender called the killing a lynching and dismissed the mob's claim that the brothers had insulted two Jewish girls as a pretext.

The brothers lived at 2029 West 13th Street, near the corner where they were attacked. According to the St. Paul Appeal, Black residents who could not find housing elsewhere in Chicago had begun moving into the "ghetto" and had been ordered out by Jewish residents. When they refused to leave, the Appeal wrote, two Jewish girls said they had been insulted by "negroes," and the riot followed.

The Defender's account held that the brothers, on leaving a streetcar at Robey Street, were jostled by a crowd of drinking men "looking for trouble." While the mob severely beat James, Charles ran away and reached home. The surviving text of what followed is partly illegible, but it refers to a pistol Charles had learned to use while fighting in France and states that "five members of the mob were shot by Charles Jackson." Charles was afterward killed, and the Defender insisted that he had died "not by a fall, as was previously stated." Police stopped the mob and arrested James Jackson.

Charles Jackson's body was taken to the undertaker Geo. O. Jones on West Lake Street, where crowds came to view it in such numbers that Jones called officers to direct them. No report of an arrest of any mob member, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Defender ran the story on its front page under the headline "Robey Street Mob Slays Innocent Man" and the subhead "Charles Jackson Meets Death at Hands of White Hoodlums." It called the assault deliberate and premeditated, cast Charles as a veteran with "Race consciousness" who meant to enjoy the democracy he had fought for in France, and charged that police handling of mob violence often showed a disposition to sympathize with the mob. A week later, a Defender society column referred to Jackson as "lynched by some hoodlums."

The St. Paul Appeal, in an editorial paragraph that named no one, described the episode as the latest of several Chicago race riots and "something of a novelty." It blamed Jewish residents who had "forgot all about their persecutions in Europe" and reported one colored man dead and five white men wounded. The Appeal printed the same paragraph again on July 12.

The two Black papers gave different causes: the Defender said a drunken crowd picked the fight and used the insult story as cover, while the Appeal traced the clash to a housing conflict in which the girls' complaint set off the riot. The Defender, a local paper that named the victims and their address, is the closer source, and the two accounts are not exclusive. An earlier version attributing Charles Jackson's death to a fall is known only from the Defender's denial of it.

reader.title: Lynching of Charles Jackson
bases: A mob of white men assaulted two Black brothers in a Chicago street after an alleged insult to two Jewish girls, and one brother, Charles Jackson, was killed; the Defender called it a lynching (A1, A3).

The Defender reports that a white mob killed Charles Jackson after accusing the brothers of insulting two Jewish girls, and later calls him 'lynched' (A1, A3); the Appeal's riot account agrees on one Black man dead (A2). The verdict stays 'probable' because the surviving Defender text is garbled on how and by whom he was killed, Jackson shot five mob members first, and it mentions an earlier account that he died by a fall (A1).

The Chicago Defender (A1, A3) and the St. Paul Appeal (A2) separately report a Chicago clash triggered by a claim that two Jewish girls were insulted, ending with one Black man dead and five white men shot or wounded, though the Appeal names no one.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender report
accounts.gist: A drunken white crowd jostled the brothers as they left a streetcar and deliberately attacked them, using the claim that they had insulted two Jewish girls as a pretext; Charles shot five mob members and was afterward killed, and police arrested James.

accounts.label: St. Paul Appeal editorial
accounts.gist: Jewish residents ordered Black newcomers out of their neighborhood; when they refused, two Jewish girls said they had been insulted by 'negroes' and a riot followed, leaving one colored man dead and five white men wounded.

accounts.label: Earlier version cited by the Defender
accounts.gist: The Defender says Jackson was killed 'not by a fall, as was previously stated', implying an earlier account attributing his death to a fall; that account does not appear in the coverage.

A week later a Defender column refers to Jackson as 'lynched by some hoodlums'.
